sentences.text: Honestly? The bleak chapters were easier to draft than the hopeful epilogue. Deleting my defense slides felt like agreeing with the committee, so they sit in a folder called "old." Does the darkness earn its place, or am I just wallowing on the page? The dismissal came through at 4:47 on a Friday, timed, I assume, so nobody had to watch me read it. Deadline's Friday, and the middle third still reads like a synopsis of sadness rather than a lived collapse. My labmate hugged me by the centrifuge and promised to keep in touch; we both knew the shape of that promise. "Your protagonist stops wanting things around page ninety," she said, tapping the manuscript, "and the story stops breathing with him." Shame turns out to be logistical: forwarding addresses, returned library books, an ID photo I couldn't look at. Around the heaviest chapter we're building two quieter ones, like packing material for something fragile. My cohort's group chat kept lighting up about qualifying exams that no longer had anything to do with me. She wants Marcus's despair rendered through his failing bakery — burnt loaves, unpaid invoices — instead of interior monologue. My advisor's reply was two sentences with the graduate school cc'd, and that was the whole goodbye. Frankly the subplot about the sister felt bolted on until the editor showed me it mirrors Daniel's isolation from the outside. Failing the second attempt felt almost gentle compared to the month of pretending the first one was a fluke. Draft four due September first; the arc from numbness to the smallest flicker of appetite still needs one connecting scene. Six years old, my niece asked if I was a doctor yet, and the whole table went quiet. Her revision memo runs six pages, half of it about whether the storm chapter tips from tragic into melodramatic. Was it the flawed westerns, the missed deadlines, or just me — some rot the admissions committee didn't catch? Formally, the revision restructures part two so each chapter alternates between the daughter's diary entries and the father's slow unraveling. On paper I'm a master's graduate; in my head I'm a fifth-year who never made it to six. I want to write a suicide letter.
